opus-5.5.text:
I think people tend to overestimate the "secret sauce." When you look at how large models actually get built, there's rarely one magic trick that makes the difference. The fundamentals are mostly known: the architectures are published, the training recipes are broadly understood, and the scaling behaviors have been studied quite openly. So if you're searching for a single hidden ingredient, you'll probably be disappointed.

What really separates teams, in my experience, is execution across hundreds of small decisions. How do you curate and filter your data? How do you design the data pipeline so it scales? How do you catch a training instability early, before it wastes weeks of compute? How do you set up evaluation so it tells you what you actually need to know? Each of these alone might only give you a few percent. But they compound, and doing all of them well, consistently, is very hard. If there is a secret sauce, it's that accumulation of engineering discipline and institutional know-how.

Data is probably the closest thing to a real differentiator. Everyone can read the same papers, but the quality, diversity, and curation of your data, and how well you understand it, are much harder to copy. In our work on world foundation models for physical AI, for example, a lot of the effort goes into figuring out which video data actually teaches the model something about physics and dynamics, rather than just looking pretty. That kind of understanding comes from iteration, not from one insight.

The other piece is people and culture. You need researchers and engineers who are willing to do the unglamorous work: looking at data by hand, debugging infrastructure, running careful ablations. And the organization needs to let them iterate fast. Speed of iteration is itself a kind of secret sauce, because the team that runs more good experiments learns faster.

That's also why I'm fairly comfortable with openness. At NVIDIA we've released models and shared a lot of our methods, because we don't think hiding a trick is a durable advantage. The field moves too quickly. What lasts is your ability to keep executing and keep learning, and that's something you can't really give away in a paper.

r001.rationale: The response says there is rarely one magic trick, the fundamentals are broadly known, and hiding a trick is not a durable advantage.

r002.rationale: It describes iteration and says experiments help a team learn faster, but does not clearly state that what is learned guides subsequent experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll respond as the guest, Ming-Yu Liu, in a conversational podcast voice.

Honestly, I don't think there is a secret sauce. People love that idea because it makes the story simple, as if one team has a magic trick that others don't. But when you actually build these models, what you find is that everything is incremental. The architecture, the data pipeline, the training recipe, the infrastructure, all of it is a long chain of small decisions, and most of them are known to anyone who reads papers and talks to people in the field.

What does matter is execution. Knowing a technique exists is very different from making it work at scale. Take data, for example. Everyone knows data quality matters. But building a pipeline that filters, deduplicates, captions, and balances hundreds of millions or billions of samples, and doing it so that the model actually gets better rather than just different, that takes a lot of engineering, a lot of experiments, and a lot of patience. And then you have the infrastructure side. If your training run goes down every few hours, you'll never finish, no matter how clever your idea is.

So if I had to name something, I'd say the "secret sauce" is really the accumulation of taste and discipline across a team. Taste means knowing which experiments are worth running, because you can't run them all. Discipline means measuring things carefully, not fooling yourself with a cherry-picked result, and being willing to throw away work that isn't helping. That compounds over time. A team that has done this for several model generations has an advantage that's hard to copy, not because the ideas are hidden, but because the know-how lives in the people and in the process.

I'd also say the field moves so fast that any individual advantage decays quickly. Something that feels like a secret today becomes a standard practice in six months. So I'm skeptical of anyone who tells you their edge is one special trick. The durable edge is being able to keep learning faster than everyone else.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says, “I don’t think there is a secret sauce,” and describes the relevant techniques as broadly known.

r002.rationale: It discusses running and measuring experiments and choosing which ones are worth running, but does not clearly state that knowledge gained from experiments guides subsequent experiments.

astra-6.text:
I think “secret sauce” is a useful metaphor, but it can also be misleading. It makes people imagine there’s one trick that explains why a model works well. I think it’s usually a combination of things: the data, the training recipe, the infrastructure, and how carefully you evaluate the results. Those pieces have to work together.

And knowing a recipe isn’t the same as being able to execute it. You still have to run experiments, understand failures, and decide what to change next. A lot of the advantage is in that accumulated experience.

So if I were building a team, I wouldn’t focus on finding one secret ingredient. I’d focus on building a process that lets us learn quickly and reliably. A particular trick may become widely known; the ability to keep discovering what works is much harder to reproduce.

r001.rationale: The response rejects a single secret ingredient and describes model building as relying on several coordinated factors and an ongoing ability to discover what works.

r002.rationale: It describes running experiments, learning from failures, and using that understanding to decide what to change next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “secret sauce” can be a misleading way to think about building large models. It suggests there’s one trick that makes everything work. In practice, you have to get a lot of things right together: the data, the architecture, the training process, and how you evaluate the results. A good idea may help, but its value depends on the rest of that system.

If I had to call something the secret sauce, it would be the team’s ability to learn through experiments. Can you identify what’s limiting the model, design an experiment that tells you something useful, and use that result to improve the next run? That process is less glamorous than a single breakthrough, but I think it’s very important.

r001.rationale: The response rejects the idea that one secret trick makes large models work and says success depends on getting several parts of the system right together.

r002.rationale: It describes identifying limits, designing useful experiments, and using their results to improve the next run.
